name: Mesh
baseline: jemalloc (Firefox, Redis); glibc malloc (SPEC CPU2006, Ruby)
workload: Resident set size over Firefox Speedometer 2.0, Redis 4.0 with fragmentation, Ruby and SPECint2006, with runtime overhead measured alongside.
claimed_speedup: Memory, not speed: Firefox 530 MB vs 632 MB under bundled jemalloc (-16%), Redis -39% (paper abstract), SPECint2006 geomean memory -2.4% vs glibc; runtime cost about 1% for Firefox, geomean 0.7% overhead on SPECint2006
compiler_and_flags: Mesh built with gcc 8 -O3 -flto; SPEC built with clang 4.0 -O2
hardware: MacBook Pro, Intel i7-5600U, 16 GiB RAM, Linux 4.18, Ubuntu Bionic
tradeoffs: Linux and macOS 64-bit only; works through LD_PRELOAD; meshing costs a small amount of runtime and uses virtual-memory remapping tricks.
caveats: Claim is memory reduction at roughly equal speed, not faster execution. Paper numbers are from 2018 hardware and old allocator versions (jemalloc 3.6.0, gperftools 2.5). Paper is PLDI-reviewed, but the benchmark harness (mstat and Firefox setup) was not confirmed public here, so B rather than A.
found_via: Blogs / talks (personal and company engineering blogs, conference talks): WebSearch 'Mesh allocator plasma-umass compacting memory allocator github'; paper PDF read from the repo via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: fc_malloc
workload: 128-byte allocations and frees, single thread and 10 threads.
claimed_speedup: Single-threaded 2.6 s vs 5.8 s glibc and 4.5 s jemalloc; 10 threads 6.8 s vs 18.2 s glibc and 13.6 s jemalloc
tradeoffs: Experimental lock-free design based on LMAX-disruptor ideas; no license file found; likely not production hardened.
caveats: First-party README table with a single 128-byte workload; no compiler, flags or CPU stated; jemalloc version unknown; repo untouched since 2013.
found_via: Blogs / talks (personal and company engineering blogs, conference talks): WebSearch 'Qt fast and thread-safe pool allocator github source' surfaced the repo

name: v8malloc
workload: Microbenchmarks MB-01 to MB-06: single-thread 8-byte alloc, 8-thread scalability, mixed workload, fragmentation RSS, 256 MiB allocation p99 latency.
claimed_speedup: 8-thread 296.4 M ops/s vs 295.2 glibc, 290.8 tcmalloc, 271.3 jemalloc, 217.5 mimalloc; 8-byte 22 ns/op vs 23 glibc, 26 jemalloc, 32 mimalloc; 256 MiB alloc p99 1 us vs 160 us mimalloc, 8 us jemalloc
tradeoffs: Linux only; early-stage; AddressSanitizer unsupported, ThreadSanitizer experimental.
caveats: Wins are mostly margins under 5 percent on a tiny set of microbenchmarks; README itself shows it behind tcmalloc on mixed workload (11.50 vs 22.26 M ops/s), about 3x slower on 16-256 KiB allocations, and behind mimalloc on producer-consumer. Author states main internals still being implemented. Tier A assumes bench/ code and scripts reproduce the table; not run.
found_via: Blogs / talks (personal and company engineering blogs, conference talks): WebSearch 'github memory allocator outperforms tcmalloc jemalloc mimalloc benchmark'

name: FastAlloc
workload: 33 throughput comparisons across block sizes plus tail latency and memory retention, thread-caching slab allocator.
claimed_speedup: Wins 20/33 throughput comparisons vs glibc, 21/33 vs jemalloc, 12/33 vs mimalloc; small blocks 1.24-2.98x faster; memory retention 16.0 MB vs 46.7 MB glibc, 171.8 MB jemalloc, 552.2 MB mimalloc
hardware: 2-vCPU VM (CPU model not stated), measured 2026-09-10, median of 5 runs
tradeoffs: Drop-in malloc replacement with lock-free TLS caches; very new, small user base.
caveats: Loses most comparisons against mimalloc (12 of 33 wins); CPU model not stated so below tier A; 2-vCPU VM limits multithread conclusions; last commit message is a restore to an older baseline.
found_via: Blogs / talks (personal and company engineering blogs, conference talks): WebSearch 'new C++ memory allocator faster than mimalloc benchmark github'

name: fast-alloc
workload: 64-byte allocations: pool, stack and free-list allocators against new/delete, frame workloads.
claimed_speedup: Pool allocators 3.0-14.9x faster than new/delete; stack allocators 2.4-20.1x for allocation/reset and 7.0-24.0x for frame workloads; free-list 1.0-6.7x
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2.0 -O3 -march=native (Linux); Apple Clang 21.0 and MSVC 19.51 Release
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 8700GE (Linux); Apple Silicon arm64; Windows CI runner
tradeoffs: Specialised fixed-size pool, stack and free-list allocators for game code, not general-purpose malloc replacements.
caveats: Compares special-purpose arenas and pools with the general system allocator, which is a weak baseline (no jemalloc or mimalloc comparison); tier A assumes the repo's benchmark code reproduces the table; not run.
found_via: Blogs / talks (personal and company engineering blogs, conference talks): WebSearch 'new C++ memory allocator faster than mimalloc benchmark github'

name: elfmalloc (allocators-rs)
workload: threadtest, shbench and producer-consumer benchmarks from 1 to 32 threads.
claimed_speedup: Highest throughput on threadtest small objects except at 32 threads where it trails jemalloc, and similar leadership on shbench; no single ratio stated on the page (qualitative from plots)
hardware: Dual Xeon E5-2620v4, 16 cores / 32 threads, under WSL
tradeoffs: Rust implementation, usable from C/C++ only through its C API or LD_PRELOAD; frequently uses more memory than competitors; compared against jemalloc dev version from August 2017.
caveats: First-party results run on WSL, compiler flags not stated, results are plot-based; old baselines (glibc 2.19); unmaintained since 2020; mimalloc not compared.
found_via: Blogs / talks (personal and company engineering blogs, conference talks): WebSearch 'github memory allocator outperforms tcmalloc jemalloc mimalloc benchmark'

name: Exgen-Malloc
baseline: mimalloc, dlmalloc (glibc malloc lineage), jemalloc, tcmalloc
workload: Single-threaded applications: SPEC CPU2017, redis-benchmark and mimalloc-bench, allocator built by stripping multithread metadata from mimalloc.
claimed_speedup: 1.17x geomean over dlmalloc and 1.05x over mimalloc on SPEC CPU2017; memory savings over mimalloc of 6.2% (SPEC CPU2017), 0.1% (redis-benchmark), 25.2% (mimalloc-bench)
tradeoffs: Only for single-threaded programs; about 2,000 lines of C/C++.
caveats: Snippet only: the arXiv, IEEE and utexas.edu pages were blocked by the egress policy, so numbers come from search result summaries, not an opened page. No public repo found. Peer-reviewed, so a later check could move it to B if the paper is reachable.
found_via: Blogs / talks (personal and company engineering blogs, conference talks): WebSearch 'memory allocator design performance engineering blog beating malloc jemalloc' result 'Old is Gold: Optimizing Single-threaded Applications with Exgen-Malloc'

name: Bloodmoon001 memory-allocator
workload: Fixed-size pool allocator: single int allocate+free, std::string create+destroy, bulk 10,000 allocations.
claimed_speedup: Single int 2,731 ns vs 29,067 ns malloc (10.6x); std::string 2.7x; bulk 10,000 allocations 7.9x; 188M ops/s vs 23M ops/s
tradeoffs: Header-only fixed-size pool, not a general-purpose allocator.
caveats: 29 microseconds for a single malloc is implausibly slow, suggesting harness artifacts; baseline is the Windows CRT malloc, not a modern allocator; 3 commits, toy-scale project.
found_via: Blogs / talks (personal and company engineering blogs, conference talks): WebSearch 'new C++ memory allocator faster than mimalloc benchmark github'
